newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to insist on strict EMU compliance - Hauser.
newsitem.headline: Germany to insist on strict EMU compliance - Hauser.

text.p: Germany will insist on a strict interpretation of the Maastricht treaty when it comes to choosing which countries qualify for Europe's single currency, a senior Finance Ministry official said on Thursday.
"The government will insist on a strict interpretation of the criteria," finance state secretary Hansgeorg Hauser said according to the text of a speech he gave in Duesseldorf.
"Even a hint of doubt in the markets over the stability of the euro could endanger the project," Hauser, who is a member of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) party, said.

Hauser said there was no disagreement among Germany's partners in the European Union over the demand by his country's parliament and constitutional court that the Maastricht criteria should be strictly applied.
"This is essential to achieve sustainable convergence. One-off efforts which take effect only in 1997 are not enough," Hauser said.

Germany has pledged to cut its budget deficit exactly in line with the Maastricht target of three percent of gross domestic product this year. Its main partner, France, has a deficit running at around 3.5 percent and will probably have to make use of the treaty's leeway to qualify for EMU.
Hauser said that there were "significant shortcomings" in the efforts by European countries to contain borrowing.
"Therefore state finances must, both in Germany and elsewhere, be continued with full force," he said.

"We must not waste our time. Moreover, we must be more determined than ever to work towards joining EMU on January 1, 1999," he said, adding. "In case of doubt, convergence comes before the timetable."

Hauser stressed that no country enjoyed an automatic right to qualify for EMU. He said the creation of a remodelled exchange rate mechanism for countries not joining the first wave of EMU membership would help close "convergence gaps".

"Fulfilling the criteria remains decisive. Those who do not make enough progress in their convergence efforts in time for the currency union will, if necessary in their own interests, still need a flexible exchange rate against the euro," he said.
